title: Southport survivors' parents 'disgusted' by school recovery funding
description: Parents of children injured in the Southport knife attack have criticised "huge discrepancies" in support money given to schools in the area after the
body: Parents of children injured in the Southport knife attack have criticised "huge discrepancies" in support money given to schools in the area after the stabbing.Schools attended by 10 of the survivors received more than a million pounds in recovery funding between them, while schools attended by 13 other survivors received no direct funding, the families' lawyers have said.Council documents, external published this afternoon reveal that £1,013,920 has been allocated to seven schools in the Sefton local authority area following the attack in July 2024.The council says it was up to schools to tell it of the help and funding they needed, as seven local schools have done.​​The largest recipient was Churchtown Primary School, which was given £546,815. It was attended by two of the girls who were killed, as well as children who survived.The council also allocated £52,360 to Presfield High School and Specialist College, which was attended by the attacker, Axel Rudakubana.Three girls - Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe and Alice da Silva Aguiar - were murdered in what was described as the worst mass stabbing in modern British history.Twenty-three girls survived the attack, which happened at a Taylor Swift-themed dance and yoga workshop for children.The mother of a girl the BBC has been calling Daisy, who was seven when she was stabbed 33 times in the attack, said she was "horrified" by the differences in funding."We have had to fight for every penny to support our daughter, and none of it has come from this fund," she said."To know that we have had such a private, anonymous, invisible battle to get our daughter the most basic support and care she needs at school, and that it has been provided by other local authorities, while Sefton Council was handing out over half a million pounds to a single school just makes me feel incredibly angry and sad."She said that the council should have approached every school attended by children who were present at the attack and ensured that they had fair access to support.The mother of two other surviving girls said that she was "absolutely disgusted"."The council never spoke to us or asked us what we needed, meanwhile our daughters have been passed from pillar to post, moving schools to try and get the help they needed in class after everything they had been through," she said.The elder daughter, whom we are calling Sarah, spoke to BBC Panorama last year. Aged 14 at the time of the attack, she was seriously wounded but managed to lead several other children, including her young sister, to safety. The girls' father added: "Nobody is suggesting schools shouldn't have received funding. Nor should anyone question the importance of remembering the children whose lives were lost."But what about those who survived; the children who were physically injured; those who witnessed the unimaginable; those who are still struggling with their education, their mental health and everyday life."Nicola Ryan-Donnelly, of Fletchers Solicitors, which represents 22 of the 23 surviving children, said the disparity in funding is "shameful and outrageous"."Eye-watering sums have been handed out to single schools, while six schools attended by 13 surviving girls we represent received absolutely nothing from this pot," she said.She accused Sefton Council of having "completely failed in its due diligence" to establish where money and support were most needed.A spokesperson for Sefton Council said: "The children, families and school communities affected by the events of July 2024 remain at the heart of Southport's recovery and support of course continues."The council said that it had initially made support available across Southport schools, with additional funding for those facing specific pressures arising from the attack.It added that "schools who came to the council with additional needs were asked to provide specific information about what they required" and that "allocations varied based on the type of help required by those schools."The council also said that the individual school grants were only one part of a wider response, which included increasing capacity in children and family services across the local authority.

schema.headline: Southport survivors' parents 'disgusted' by school recovery funding

title: Record 5,200 heat-linked deaths estimated in England this year
description: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, An estimated 5,258 deaths in England were associated with this summer's hot weatherByDan WoodlandUpdated
body: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, An estimated 5,258 deaths in England were associated with this summer's hot weatherByDan WoodlandUpdated 2 hours agoMore than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.The UKHSA said summer 2026 was "exceptional", and that it recorded the highest annual number of heat episodes, which it defines as days when the average Central England Temperature (CET) is at least 20C. There were seven heat episodes between May and August, adding up to a total of 41 days. A summer of persistent heatThe UK experienced widespread heatwaves as 2026 became the hottest summer on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.A heatwave in May smashed the temperature record for that month by more than 2C, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens.A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.Both were caused by heat domes - stalled areas of high pressure that trap hot air over the region.Another heatwave in mid-August saw temperatures climb as high as 38.2C at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire, making it the hottest day of the year.The UK's hottest day on record was 19 July 2022, when temperatures hit 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire.A lack of rainfall this year also saw droughts declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires caused devastation in some parts of the country.UKHSA said the findings "underline the need for longer-term adaptation" to a warming climate, and that adapting homes, neighbourhoods and health and care settings would be "increasingly important".Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental health scientist at UKHSA, said this summer's hot weather had a substantial impact on public health, "particularly during the early heat episodes in May and June".He added that periods of extreme heat are expected to become "longer, more frequent and more intense" as the climate continues to warm.Speaking in the Commons, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she wanted "to offer the deepest condolences to all those who lost a loved one this summer"."The numbers are a stark reminder of the human impact of climate change, and that is why I have asked the NHS to now prepare for summer as seriously as we do for winter," she said.During a speech at the COP31 summit earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke about the extreme weather experienced in the UK this summer, describing it as "not normal".

schema.headline: Record 5,200 heat-linked deaths estimated in England this year

title: French ex-President Nicolas Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to be tried next year
description: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for c
body: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy. The pair deny any wrongdoing.Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president. Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face the charge of "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised group and receiving stolen goods related to witness tampering". They deny any wrongdoing.

schema.headline: French ex-President Nicolas Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to be tried next year

title: What Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia teaches China's Xi about Trump
description: Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world  - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's
body: Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world  - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets. But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China. That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too. Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt". Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing. Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points. For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented. The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy. But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.   Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December. Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage. He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared  to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over. Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers. Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

schema.headline: What Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia teaches China's Xi about Trump

title: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
description: The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" t
body: The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations. Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot. Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.The joint alert, external between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation". Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday. Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic". "These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia. Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face". Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

schema.headline: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage

title: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it
description: Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.Every
body: Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it."I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load".The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present."If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.While paying for help with such tasks may seem a luxury, for some people support with life's everyday trials is a lifeline.Anna Allington sought help after her husband died. "My husband passed away. I was 47," she says."And the same week he passed away, I got leukaemia. There was a lot to sort out and I was very, very unwell."Anna, now 51, still suffers the after-effects of her cancer. "I can't function executively like I used to," she says.She pays £1,200 a month for 40 hours of help from Cheshire-based company Vi-Va. Her personal assistant helps her respond to emails, manage her diary and make travel plans and bookings."We meet twice a week on Zoom," says Anna, who lives in the Cotswolds, so they can go through all her tasks.

schema.headline: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it

title: Pip disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByBecky MortonPolitical reporterThe main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additi
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByBecky MortonPolitical reporterThe main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended.The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition.The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year.The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance".Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system".Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings. The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million.The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs.It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report.Giving a statement in the House of Commons, Sir Stephen said Pip "remains a vital source of support" but the system was "no longer fit for purpose". He told MPs the current assessment process was "dehumanising" and focused on "what somebody cannot do", rather than "supporting independence".The government has committed to a recommendation that people receiving end-of-life care or with "serious, well-evidenced conditions" would receive payments without a full assessment.It has also agreed to reduce "unnecessary" reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve.Under the report's proposals, cash payments would remain alongside better support to signpost people into education or employment, although claimants could choose to exchange part of their payment for practical services instead.In the longer-term, the report recommends changes to the assessment process that look at someone's real-life additional costs and individual needs, focusing on "how people can live the life they want to live, rather than what they cannot do".It proposes "improved" questions to understand the extra costs people face, although claimants would not be asked to calculate their costs or provide receipts.'Rebalancing'Currently eligibility for Pip is based on how difficult people find carrying out everyday tasks, with two levels of payment available.But the review suggests future payment options could include bands more closely linked to extra costs.The report says its approach is likely to lead to a "rebalancing" of payments, indicating that some claimants could lose out under a new system, either receiving less than they do currently or not qualifying for payments at all."Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support," it says."Conversely, this benefit is not appropriate for those who do not incur any additional costs associated with being disabled."The review also calls for an increase in face-to-face assessments, which has been show to reduce eligibility.The remit of the review was not to produce savings, and it does not set out whether the reforms would reduce the overall welfare bill.Spending on Pip is set to be about £32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to £41.5bn by the end of the decade. It comes after a separate review by former minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets).The government welcomed Milburn's report, which included a recommendation to move under-25s off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system. This has lead to concerns about a two-tier system, where some people with the same conditions could get different levels of payments depending on their age.The government has said it will consider the Timms review alongside Milburn's recommendations, with its final proposals set out early next year.Sir Stephen said this would include detailing the overall costs of changes to the system.'Months of uncertainty'Eduin Latimer, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said the review's recommendations had "the potential to better tailor Pip to claimants' needs".But he said this would also create challenges, "most importantly in defining what disability-related costs are included, and finding a fair way of measuring them".Latimer said making it easier to apply for Pip in its current form would "likely increase the number of claimants - and hence spending".He added: "If the government wants to make Pip easier to apply for while also keeping spending in line with current projections, they would likely have to tighten eligibility criteria or reduce award amounts."Disability charities have largely welcomed the review's recommendations of fast-tracked support and fewer reassessments.However, they have said any changes should not leave disabled people financially worse off.The Liberal Democrats said younger disabled people would now face "months of uncertainty" whilst the government considers the separate reviews from Timms and Milburn, and urged ministers to say quickly what they intend to do.The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales. However, the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales. Get in touchDo you claim Pip? Share your experience.

schema.headline: Pip disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs

title: Man's shock at Ryanair flight to Spain using wife's passport
description: A man who mistakenly travelled to Spain using his wife's passport has said he is still baffled about how he was able to make the trip without being st
body: A man who mistakenly travelled to Spain using his wife's passport has said he is still baffled about how he was able to make the trip without being stopped in the UK.Ben Moore, from Talke, in Staffordshire, noticed there was a problem soon after getting off his Ryanair flight while he was queuing to get his passport checked at Alicante airport."I opened up the passport there and, to my horror, it was my wife's photo on the passport," he said. "The lads who I was with basically said the colour drained out of me immediately."Third-party provider Swissport, which carries out Ryanair's checks at Manchester Airport where Moore flew from, said it was now reinforcing mandatory boarding procedures.Moore, who was travelling to Alicante on a stag party with friends, told BBC Radio Stoke he initially thought he must have picked up his wife's passport in addition to his own.He said he approached Spanish police who - along with the language barrier - appeared to be as confused as he was about how he had turned up there without his own passport."I searched through all my luggage about eight times thinking there's no way I could have got to Alicante without my own passport," he said."They could not believe that I'd got to Spain on my wife's passport."

schema.headline: Man's shock at Ryanair flight to Spain using wife's passport

title: Australia vs England: Aneurin Donald and Phil Salt star as visitors level T20 series
description: Second T20, CarraraAustralia 184-8 (20 overs): Chaudhary 45 (35); Curran 2-29 England 188-2 (13.1 overs): Donald 85 (32); Meredith 1-18England won by
body: Second T20, CarraraAustralia 184-8 (20 overs): Chaudhary 45 (35); Curran 2-29 England 188-2 (13.1 overs): Donald 85 (32); Meredith 1-18England won by eight wickets; series level 1-1ScorecardFrom Gorseinon to the Gold Coast to global recognition. Welshman Aneurin Donald's demolition of Australia in the second T20 will make the rest of the world notice his talents and pave the way for numerous franchise deals, according to former England captain Michael Vaughan.Donald's astonishing opening partnership of 151 in 10 overs with Phil Salt helped England hammer Australia and levelled the T20 series on the Gold Coast, as they chased 184 in just 13.1 overs.Donald blitzed 85 from 32 balls, including nine sixes, while his compatriot Salt made 58 off 30 as the pair from small Welsh villages in Swansea and Denbighshire took the Australians apart. Donald's 18-ball fifty was the joint third-fastest for England in the format as the pair raced to 79-0 in the powerplay, flogging Australia's second-string bowling attack to all corners of the ground in a remarkable display of power hitting."It was a night where we saw a player really step up to the big stage," Vaughan told BBC Sport."I'm sure we're going to see much more over the next few years from Donald, but I think tonight the rest of the world noticed and said 'oh, there's a player there'."He's got a few franchise gigs at the moment but to do it on the biggest stage against Australia, with the world watching, he's going to be talked about." His opening partner Salt, who was dropped by Joel Davies on 10, was mostly able to watch from the non-striker's end before accelerating to a 24-ball half-century of his own, which came during a brutal over from spinner Davies that went for 31. Donald looked gutted to miss out on a century after he holed out to long-on off Riley Meredith's bowling, before Salt was brilliantly caught and bowled by Ben Dwarshuis an over later. However, England's phenomenal top order - which still awaits the return of Jos Buttler from injury - finished the job with ease as Tom Banton walked off unbeaten on 26 off eight balls, including a monstrous six for the winning runs.Australia's 184-8 looked competitive on a surface that had assisted England's spinners and Sam Curran's slower balls - the hosts recovering from a stodgy middle over period after falling to 58-4 in the powerplay. Davies added a handy cameo of 38 before Dwarshuis whacked Curran's last three balls for six to finish strongly but within just a few overs of the chase, Donald and Salt had silenced a lively Australian crowd in style.The five-match series continues at the Gabba, Brisbane, on Friday.Donald made his T20 international debut as a 29-year-old earlier this summer on the back of consistent county and Hundred performances, but struggled to really cement his place with 56 runs in four innings. Still, a player known for an incredible strike-rate in particular, he was backed by Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum to play freely and showcased that strength against an Australia attack that had no answers. "He's the perfect T20 striker," Vaughan added. "He has got a great base and a good eye and he doesn't over-complicate it. His mindset is to just try and hit everything for six, very much the modern T20 player. "The game is moving forward and you need players like Donald who can hit the ball like that." Brook himself said he was "speechless" at the end of the game, high praise from one of the world's best, as Donald and Salt made what could have been a tricky chase look like a stroll in the park. Only three international T20s had been held at the Gold Coast's Carrara Oval previously so England were in relatively unknown territory.Not that it mattered to Donald, who swatted Davies for four from his first ball to start the demolition. His first couple of sixes off Jack Edwards sailed into the crowd despite looking like he had not timed them perfectly, giving Australia captain Mitch Marsh an insight into his new Perth Scorchers team-mate when the Big Bash League starts in December.Though the pitch had looked difficult to face spin in Australia's innings, Donald and Salt both tucked into it with aplomb - before Salt's takedown of Davies, Donald clubbed Nikhil Chaudhary for 26 to bring up his fifty by the end of the fifth over. Donald's showcase gives England a nice headache at the top of the order, with Buttler and Jacob Bethell still to come back into the fold - a frightening prospect for opposition bowlers.Despite the batting brilliance, there were mixed fortunes for England's bowlers with a contrast between their spinners and seamers.Australia's powerplay was bizarre. Their run-rate was healthy, just shy of 10 runs an over, but they threw away four wickets which meant they had to be more cautious throughout the middle. Marsh was caught and bowled by Henry Crocombe, Jake Fraser-McGurk was out slogging to Curran before debutant James Coles produced a fine run out to get rid of Sam Harper. Coles then took the catch in the deep to get rid of Tim David, and that allowed the masterful Adil Rashid and Liam Dawson to get to work, bowling seven overs on the bounce as Australia's middle order came to a standstill. Rashid tied Lachlan Shaw and Joel Davies in knots early on as they struggled to pick up his variations before he removed the former for a stodgy 10 from 17 balls. Davies dug in before accelerating at the death, with assistance from the big-hitting Edwards as Jamie Overton's struggles continued. The 18th over conceded 16 as he only bowled two overs for 28, before Crocombe's penultimate over flew for 16 and Dwarshuis got to work on Curran, who was also taken apart in the final over in Australia's win on Saturday. Unfortunately for Curran, he had previously been sensational at mixing up his pace deceptively and had figures of 2-9 off his first three, but completely lost control of his yorkers in the final three balls which the powerful Dwarshuis sent flying. England will be grateful for the return of Jofra Archer to their ranks as their difficulties at closing out an innings are becoming a concern.

schema.headline: Australia vs England: Aneurin Donald and Phil Salt star as visitors level T20 series

title: Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByElla KiplingFreya Scott-Turner and Robby Westin SandringhamUpdated 2 hours agoTwo men have been arrested on suspicion of b
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByElla KiplingFreya Scott-Turner and Robby Westin SandringhamUpdated 2 hours agoTwo men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass at the Prince and Princess of Wales's country home on the Sandringham estate, police say.Norfolk Police said it received a call just before 18:00 GMT on Monday following a report of suspicious activity at Anmer Hall.Police deployed dogs, drones and a helicopter to search the area and arrested two men on the estate, who remain in custody.The property was unoccupied at the time, police added. Kensington Palace said it did not comment on security matters.William and Catherine do not live at Anmer Hall full-time, but use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays.Val Blackmur, an 83-year-old resident who lives on the road leading up to the house, told the BBC it was "amazing" if anybody had been "stupid" enough to try breaking in.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Prince and Princess of Wales do not live at Anmer Hall full-timeThe country retreat, which has 10 bedrooms, was a gift to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II following their wedding in 2011.The red brick Georgian mansion is on the private Sandringham estate in Norfolk and is about two miles (3km) east from Sandringham House, one of the King's private residences.The Prince and Princess's main home is on the Windsor Castle estate in Berkshire.The Sandringham estate spans approximately 31 sq miles (80 sq km).Members of the public can visit it, although the house and its gardens are currently closed.The Royal Parkland, which is the woodland to the west of the main house, is open to the public all year round. Many other members of the Royal Family also live on the estate, including Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who moved on to Marsh Farm in February. Despite tight security around members of the Royal Family, there have been several intrusions on their property in recent decades.One of the more recent incidents was in 2024, when Thames Valley Police said burglars had broken into a farm on the Windsor Castle estate and stolen two vehicles.Image source, Robby West/BBCImage caption, Val Blackmur said in all the 50 years she had lived near Anmer Hall, she had not heard of a break-in happening in the areaBlackmur said: "We never seem to have any trouble so when something out of the ordinary happens that sort of makes you prick your ears up and think, what was all that about?"The 83-year-old said it was not unusual to hear police cars or helicopters in the area. "We've lived here 50 years now... we've never heard nothing like that," she said."Up at Anmer Hall it's so secluded and out of the way, not in full view - I should think people would be shocked."Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home

title: The Timms review into Pip disability benefits - key takeaways
description: First the short term. A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route
body: First the short term. A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible.Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments.Then the long term.Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit.Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level.A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse.The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals.The inquiry was not set up to find savings in the system despite the fact that spending on Pip is forecast to cost more than £40bn by 2030. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.The report acknowledges that since the benefit was introduced, the number of people receiving disability benefits has increased across every age group for both men and women. Most of the increase has happened between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest increases among young people aged 16-19, people in their 30s and women, whose rates of benefit receipt have risen faster than men's.The report says that a reformed Pip system that more accurately reflects peoples' needs will likely mean "a rebalancing process". While the review didn't set out to make savings, it couldn't increase the overall costs and with some people likely to gain, others will almost certainly lose some cash. The review is not explicit on who these people might be.Separate research last month from a think tank, the Resolution Foundation, suggested that one in six Pip recipients didn't have any additional costs associated with their conditions. In an interview to coincide with the review, Timms said that "if people don't have extra costs, then this is not the benefit for them".

schema.headline: The Timms review into Pip disability benefits - key takeaways

title: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'
description: Sir David Pearson, chair of the Supported Housing Advisory Panel and social care expert, has been appointed to lead the investigation.The government a
body: Sir David Pearson, chair of the Supported Housing Advisory Panel and social care expert, has been appointed to lead the investigation.The government added the investigation would examine the scale of the problems in the city's SEA sector, including the quality of accommodation and support, use of public money, and effectiveness of oversight and regulation.In a letter confirming the appointment, housing secretary Angela Rayner asked Pearson to lead a "rapid independent investigation" into the claims.She said the investigation should focus on Birmingham, given consistent reports that the area was at the "epicentre of concerns" about poor-quality supported accommodation, while considering the extent to which any findings can be applied to the rest of the country."Good-quality supported housing can turn lives around and provide people with the support they need to live as independently as possible," Rayner wrote. "There are increasing reports, however, that this system is being abused, with vulnerable people exploited at the expense of the taxpayer."SEA is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse. In many cases it works well for people, but BBC investigations over the past five years have uncovered stories of vulnerable people, including care leavers and people with mental health problems, being let down by the system designed to support them.Some residents said they had been left living alongside drug dealers and criminals, and fearing for their lives, despite some providers reportedly claiming more than £200 a week at the time for every person they house.Supported housing expenditure had risen faster in Birmingham than the national average in recent years, a government spokesperson said.Pat McFadden, Work and Pensions Secretary, said there were "real concerns" about how the system was operating."Sir David's investigation will get to the bottom of what's going on, and where we find wrongdoing, we will act to make sure money is spent on supporting people who need it," he said.The council paid out £404.4m for SEA in the 2024-25 financial year, with a further £211.8m paid between April and July 2026.More than 34,000 people in the city currently live in SEA, compared to about 22,000 living in London, despite its population being more than seven times larger.The BBC has previously heard evidence of claims that some housing providers were willing to make benefit claims for people who did not live in their properties.The council introduced controls, requiring SEA providers to submit evidence they were delivering more than minimal care to their tenants.But a recent internal audit showed the authority could not show the review had been completed for 72% of the claims tested. At the time the results were published, 12,700 live cases were waiting review, of which around 7,100 had exceeded the six-month limit.Bosses said a plan was in place to reduce the backlog to zero by the end of the year.Preet Gill, the Labour MP for Birmingham Edgbaston, said she welcomed the independent review."I have campaigned on exempt accommodation for nearly a decade and worked with residents, the council and police to shut down Saif Lodge, the first exempt accommodation property in the country to be closed in 2021," she said."Neighbours have had enough of the antisocial behaviour, and vulnerable people are being let down while some providers profit."It is not the first time politicians have investigated the issue.An inquiry by the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee in 2022 reported that some vulnerable people had faced rape and exploitation by landlord "gangsters" in England's "complete mess" of an exempt housing system.That was two years after Birmingham was named as one of five pilot projects, external designed to improve quality, enforcement, oversight and value for money in the sector.Alysha told Panorama that she had moved into SEA 18 months ago, a survivor of domestic abuse.She had nowhere to go and no family living nearby, so she was made homeless and relying on universal credit."I never thought I'd be homeless and I never thought my marriage would break down, but it did," she said."I felt extremely alone. I needed help getting myself back on to my feet, and that's how I got myself into supported accommodation." She has since lived in three different SEA properties but admitted her experience was far from the fresh start she needed. Alysha was forced to leave her first placement after just six months."There was one day at about 05:30 in the morning, where I was woken up to screaming and growling and banging. "They'd been fighting really badly. The house was covered in blood, police were called, and the house was no longer safe." Jane and Melvin, residents living in Selly Oak, said the house next door to them was converted into SEA. The couple admit at times they felt unsafe in their own home with the tenants of the property having involvement with guns, knives, and drugs. "There were people overdosing," Jane recalled, adding: "Twice the front door was kicked in by people who didn't live there."Jane said she and her husband never objected to the property being used to support people in need. But she felt as though those living in the SEA were left to run "amuck"."I think they were lacking the support that they needed, really," she explained.

schema.headline: Government launches inquiry into Birmingham housing scheme 'exploitation'

title: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
description: As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well
body: As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns. The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act. In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.  The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this. They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

schema.headline: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away

title: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
description: Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media v
body: Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online. Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Badenoch said she had been "pretty shocked" by the videos coming out of the event, questioning whether they were in good taste.She said that while Burnham might think he was connecting with young people, many people around the world "will think our country is a joke".She said: "I do think Andy Burnham should apologise for the way he is using Number 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks."Vladimir Putin, President Xi and all sorts of other people who are hostile to the UK will see these things, they will get reports of them, and they will see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country."In a reference to Balegde's video, she said: "I think it is a disgrace that Number 10 – that door which is a symbol of British democracy, power and authority in the world, dignity, that's where we receive people like President Zelensky, showing them that they have the support of people in this country, is being degraded in this way."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also criticised the use of the Downing Street door as "puerile" and "demeaning" but said he wouldn't ban influencers from Number 10."I wouldn't let them behave quite the way that it happened," he said. "It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed."Responding to questions about Balegde's video, the prime minister's spokesperson said "the content was clearly not acceptable", but added "content creators are responsible for what they choose to post".Asked repeatedly whether Number 10 had requested for the video be removed, the spokesperson said: "It is right the creator took down that content."It's clearly not acceptable and that is reflected by the fact that it has been taken down."They also defended the decision to invite influencers to Downing Street, saying it was "right that the PM listens to" social media content creators who "reach millions of people who don't get their news from traditional media".Balegde also gave a speech inside the influencers' event, which was held by Burnham in an attempt to build links with a growing sector of the economy.A smaller group of creators were asked to arrive early to film videos with the prime minister.One attendee in this group said they had to run ideas past the prime minister's team for approval.A government spokesperson said they would not comment on security and whether the footage captured on the government phones was reviewed, but said it was "not abnormal" for attendees of Downing Street to use government phones.

schema.headline: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
